before.name: Southwest Ridge
before.overview: Easiest access when snow closes the Summit Lake road, and a handy way in for skiers after the bowls beneath the top. The trailhead at Pioneer Gulch gives a round trip of 7.5 miles and gains somewhat over 4000 feet. Hike until the trail joins the one named for Diamond Peak, then go directly uphill bearing climbers left to the southwest ridge. Stay on it until it merges with the south ridge, and continue to the top.
what_to_bring: ice axe and crampons — may be needed
pro_tips: In late April an early start finds snow firm enough to climb in boots, with crampons needed only for the upper third.
watch_out: In mid-May the forest between about 6,000 and 7,000 ft is confusing, and a snowshoe track there can melt out.
In mid-May the snow on the final summit ridge swings between firm and postholing; safe but unforgiving off line.
before.approach: Start at the Pioneer Gulch trailhead and follow the Pioneer Gulch Trail until it meets the Diamond Peak Trail. Leave the trail there and head straight uphill, trending toward climber's left, until you reach the southwest ridge. In winter, with the Summit Lake road shut, this is the easiest line to reach. In mid-May snow can still cover the forest road from about 4,900 ft, adding road miles on snowshoes, while the first mile of trail is often already bare.

before.name: East Ridge
before.overview: A well-established trail leads from the parking lot, meeting the PCT after 1.1 miles. Continue on the climbers trail past a second PCT junction (heading north) by staying straight. About 3 miles of good flowing trail precede the technical ground, where rocky footing, big step-ups and big drops lead to the East Ridge. Plod up the ridge to the last 600ft, a scree (or snow) slope ending at a large, pointed summit.
pro_tips: White dots and arrows are painted on the rock through the maze section; they stop about 250 ft below the top, so follow the ridge to the summit.
Roughly two miles in the middle are nearly flat, so the steep part comes late; start early to be off the loose upper mountain in daylight.
In early July a snowfield below the summit gave a glissade descent, but it ends well away from the trail; check where it lands.
watch_out: A canal crossing near the start has no bridge; in early July it is crossed on logs.
In July the tread fades in the upper scree and braids; pick your own line and watch for painted marks.
In early July bugs are bad below treeline and ease higher up.
before.approach: From the trailhead parking lot a good trail runs about a mile to the first Pacific Crest Trail junction. Stay on the McLoughlin climbers trail, go straight past a second PCT junction that leads north, and follow smooth trail for a few miles before the footing turns rocky, with large step-ups. The well-worn trail leads to the East Ridge itself, and the final slope to the pointed summit is scree or snow. The trailhead charges a fee and has no camping.

before.name: South Ridge
before.detailed_rack: Pickets are possible in winter; otherwise carry nothing.
what_to_bring: Ice axe (late July to mid August, for snow on the traverse); 50-60 m rope for the Bowling Alley rappel (July to September)
pro_tips: The Bowling Alley entrance is a short narrow ramp of good rock just past the traverse; a wide loose gully means you went too far.
Descending, the Bowling Alley can be downclimbed or roped down; when waiting below a rappel, shelter in the alcove on the north side.
watch_out: Climbers kick loose rock down the scree above the Middle-North saddle and in the Bowling Alley; call out and stay out of the fall line (August).
The Terrible Traverse can keep snow patches into mid-August after heavy winters, and the ground under them is loose; later in the season it is all loose scree.
before.approach: From Pole Creek the trail runs through burned forest before an unmarked use-trail junction that is easy to blow past; camps at the moraine lakes near 7,500-8,000 ft shorten the summit day, and water is plentiful in the moraine in August.

July.reason: In late July the traverse toward the Bowling Alley can still be frozen snow at dawn; kicking steps works but gives no real protection.
In late July a long steep snow slope can still fill the Red Saddle traverse, steep enough that a self-arrest is unlikely to hold; parties placed pickets or ran a fixed line.

September.reason: By early September the traverse can shrink to a small ice patch with a dirt line beside it, and Shale Lake is nearly dry.

before.name: South Side Route
before.overview: Graded as a scramble (or easy snow), it totals 12.5 miles round trip. Start from Devils Lake campground and follow the South Climb Trail (signed); a permit, self-issued, is filled out at the beginning. The path crosses loose volcanic scree all the way up. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.
what_to_bring: crampons and ice axe — when snow is present
pro_tips: The small tarn at the foot of the Lewis Glacier is a spot to refill water in August; filter it.
After gaining the crater rim, the true summit is across the crater on the far side, so allow for the extra walk along the rim.
watch_out: Biting insects are heavy below treeline in mid-July
before.approach: Start at the Devils Lake trailhead on the Cascade Lakes Highway and take the signed South Sister Climbers Trail, filling out the self-issued wilderness permit at the start. The trail crosses a footbridge over Tyee Creek, crosses the highway and climbs steeply through hemlock forest to a sandy plateau, where you go straight at the four-way junction. It passes the Moraine Lake valley and continues over loose cinder to a sandy saddle at the Lewis Glacier moraine. The round trip is roughly 11 to 12 miles.
before.descent_text: Descend the way you came, down the South Sister Climbers Trail to the Devils Lake trailhead. The upper trail is loose volcanic scree and cinder that slides underfoot, and with snow cover an ice axe and crampons may be needed. Parties who loop through Moraine Lake instead face a steep, slippery trail into the canyon, with a rugged first stretch that needs hands.
